title: They Burned Scrolls on Purpose — And It Could Unlock a Roman Library
summary:
Douglas Seiler went to unusual lengths to recreate an ancient disaster. He bought papyrus and reed pens from Egypt, plus traditional lampblack ink from Japan. Then he paid high school students to write on the papyrus using passages from Star Wars, the Bible, and a quote from the 1960s sci-fi show The Outer Limits. Finally, he burned it.

The experiment mimicked a real catastrophe. When Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E., volcanic ash buried Herculaneum, an ancient Roman city in Italy. More than a thousand papyrus scrolls in a local library were transformed into fragile, charred remains. The same eruption famously destroyed nearby Pompeii. But the disaster also created an extraordinary form of preservation: the Herculaneum collection is the only known intact library to survive from antiquity.

The problem? You can't unroll the scrolls. They crumble into black dust. So Seiler focused on the chemistry of the ink. If some ancient inks contained lead, that metal might absorb X-rays far more strongly than the surrounding carbonized papyrus. A computer could then use the scans to virtually flatten the rolled sheets and expose the hidden writing.

In a paper published Sept. 16 in PLOS ONE, Seiler and his collaborators, including several Berkeley experts, report that the strategy works. Even extremely small amounts of lead made written characters detectable with X-ray tomography, also called X-ray CT. Lead absorbed as much as 25 times more X-rays than the burned papyrus around it, causing the writing to stand out dramatically.

"With lead in the ink, you would get a huge friggin' signature," Seiler said. "They're having problems reading a lot of them because of the low contrast of carbon ink on carbon paper. We're relatively certain that if they start searching for lead, or they let us search for lead, it will help this whole process."

The researchers also found that a relatively inexpensive handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner could readily detect lead-based ink in a burned scroll. That could provide a straightforward way to screen ancient scrolls first and identify which ones are the most promising candidates for detailed X-ray CT imaging.

Only a small number of the charred scrolls from Herculaneum's Villa of the Papyri have so far been virtually opened and deciphered. None of those had first been tested for lead. Researchers have not yet carried out a systematic search for lead-based ink across the collection. However, at least one previous researcher detected lead in the ink of a fragment left over from early attempts to physically open the scrolls. Many of those attempts began after the scrolls were discovered in 1752. The results were often disastrous. Trying to unwind the carbonized rolls frequently reduced them to piles of ash, eventually prompting Italian authorities to stop the practice.

Every scroll that was successfully opened physically contained writing previously unknown to scholars. Many of those texts were works by Philodemus, an Epicurean philosopher who lived in Herculaneum roughly a century before Vesuvius erupted. Today, the surviving library consists of about 1,800 scrolls and scroll fragments held in collections in Italy, France, and England.

"Almost everything from antiquity has been destroyed," Seiler said. "There's very little left except papyrus that was in a dry climate or some works that were copied by scribes and transferred down. But some of the Herculaneum scrolls aren't copies. These are books directly from the ancient world frozen in time. They're actually from Roman intellectual circles."

For scholars who study ancient writing, the potential importance is difficult to overstate. "The value in this project is practically unquantifiable," said Berkeley archaeology graduate student Leah Packard-Grams, who consulted on the project as a papyrologist. "The stakes are the largest in the history of Greek literature."
why_it_matters: It shows how chemistry and physics can rescue knowledge that looked lost forever, and the words of ancient thinkers still shape the books, laws and ideas students read today — so unlocking more of this library could change what we know about the ancient world.

background_read: Mount Vesuvius (a volcano in southern Italy, near modern Naples) erupted in 79 C.E. and buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum; Herculaneum was hit by pyroclastic flows — fast, scorching clouds of gas and rock — that carbonized the scrolls stored in the Villa of the Papyri.

The charred scrolls were rediscovered in 1752, and early attempts to peel them open destroyed many of them, which is why the surviving collection — about 1,800 scrolls and fragments, now held in Italy, France and England — is so precious.

Philodemus was a first-century-B.C.E. Greek philosopher in the tradition of Epicurus, whose school taught that the aim of life was calm and freedom from fear; his works survived only because this library did.

PLOS ONE, where the new study appeared, is a peer-reviewed open-access science journal, and X-ray CT (tomography) is the same imaging technology hospitals use for medical scans — here used to read writing hidden inside a lump of carbon.

Since 2023 an international competition called the Vesuvius Challenge has used similar scanning plus machine learning to read words from still-rolled scrolls, showing how modern tools are being aimed at this ancient problem.

perspectives.perspective: Scholars who want the texts back
perspectives.description: For papyrologists, the new ink-detection method is a breakthrough: it could finally reveal thousands of words of Greek philosophy that no living person has read and that no later copy preserves.

Museum curators may worry that scanning campaigns put irreplaceable, dust-fragile scrolls at risk if they are handled, and that excitement could outrun the slow, careful work of protecting what remains.
The story is a neat reversal: the eruption that destroyed a city accidentally preserved a library, and modern medical imaging is now being used to read what fire wrote.
If lead ink turns out to be common, handheld scanners could sort the whole collection and target the most promising scrolls; if it is rare, the method may only unlock a handful of texts.
